cc.extrasNote: Off the walk: add them with Explore, or go on their own (Mănăștur and Grigorescu by bus 9 / taxi).
cc.helpNote: Short stay: one half-afternoon walk plus a few stops off it. Base map: OpenStreetMap named streets (a 2013 extract, so newer streets may be missing; no river, buildings or parks). Outside the city, Natural Earth roads and rail. Pins from Google Places; approximate ones are marked.

sights.name: Neolog synagogue (Deportees’ Temple)
sights.blurb: A Moorish-revival synagogue of 1887 on Str. Horea, rededicated after the war to the Jews of Cluj deported in 1944.
sights.when: Exterior any time; interior rarely open.

sights.name: Cetățuia hill: Habsburg fort and Roth’s execution site
sights.blurb: A Habsburg star fort (1715–35) on the hill over the river, a barracks and prison for 200 years, where Stephan Ludwig Roth was shot in 1849. Best view of Cluj.
sights.when: Public park, open any time; many steps; some paths broken by landslides.

sights.name: Hotel Belvedere (1970s)
sights.blurb: A late-1970s socialist luxury hotel built on top of the Habsburg fort, still running with its marble atrium and period bar.
sights.when: Working hotel: lobby and bar usually walk-in.

sights.name: Casa Tranzit (former Poale Tzedek synagogue)
sights.blurb: A small Orthodox-rite synagogue, used as a warehouse under communism, and since 1997 an independent art centre on the river bank.
sights.when: Courtyard usually reachable; interior for events and exhibitions.

sights.name: Telephone Palace (“the Silo”)
sights.blurb: Cluj’s brutalist icon (Vasile Mitrea, 1969–76): raw concrete, precast fretwork and randomly scattered “shot windows”.
sights.when: Exterior only; Orange must leave by about mid-2027.

sights.name: Hintz House: the first pharmacy (1573)
sights.blurb: Cluj’s first pharmacy opened in this house on the main square in 1573; it is now a pharmacy-history museum.

sights.name: The Shot Pillars: 1989 revolution memorial
sights.blurb: Seven bronze columns pierced with symbolic bullet holes, on the corner where 14 people were shot on 21 December 1989.

sights.name: Hotel New York / Continental: the lost literary café
sights.blurb: The 1895 grand hotel whose café was Cluj’s literary heart for half a century, the Gestapo’s seat in the war, and the place the 1989 protesters walked out of.

sights.name: Romanian Academy Library (brutalist, 1973–76)
sights.blurb: An all-prefabricated brutalist library by Eliza Fierlinger and Radu Spânu: an armoured book core wrapped in reading rooms.
sights.when: Exterior any time; reading rooms Mon–Fri 8–14 for registered readers.

sights.name: Tailors’ Bastion and Baba Novac
sights.blurb: The best-kept tower of the old walls (rebuilt 1627–29); nearby, Michael the Brave’s general Baba Novac was executed in 1601.
sights.q: Tailors’ Bastion and Baba Novac, Cluj-Napoca

sights.name: Házsongard Central Cemetery
sights.blurb: Cluj’s plague-era cemetery (after 1585): a wooded hillside of Hungarian, Saxon, Jewish and Romanian graves, mausoleums and fallen stones.

sights.name: Emil Racoviță Institute of Speleology: the world’s first
sights.blurb: Founded by law in 1920, the world’s first institute of cave science, still working in the same building, with Racoviță’s bust outside.
sights.q: Emil Racoviță Institute of Speleology, Cluj-Napoca

sights.name: Central University Library: Blaga’s exile
sights.blurb: A 1909 Secession library where the banned poet-philosopher Lucian Blaga worked as a librarian in the 1950s and translated Faust.
sights.when: Readers Mon–Sat; guided tours by booking (check bcucluj.ro).

sights.name: Casa de Cultură a Studenților (1960)
sights.blurb: A 1959–60 socialist culture palace for students, opened on the regime’s national day, with a 1,000-seat hall.
sights.when: Lobby open daily 8–22 (Google); events in the hall.
sights.q: Casa de Cultură a Studenților, Cluj-Napoca

sights.name: Croco 1960: the writers’ café, revived
sights.blurb: End the walk here: the 1960s café of writers, academics and taxi drivers, closed in 2007 and reopened on the same spot in 2018.
sights.when: Hours conflict: Mon–Fri 8–17 (own site) vs 7:30–23 (booking site).

sights.name: Makovecz Reformed Church (“the whale”)
sights.blurb: Imre Makovecz’s organic timber church (1994–2008) in the Grigorescu district, its inside like a whale’s ribcage.

sights.name: Mănăștur estate and Calvaria Church lookout
sights.blurb: Cluj’s giant 1970s housing estate, built for the CUG machine plant over a demolished village; climb to the medieval Calvaria Church to look over it.
sights.q: Mănăștur estate and Calvaria Church lookout, Cluj-Napoca

sights.name: Strada Mehedinți: the S-shaped street
sights.blurb: One snaking street of Mănăștur blocks with almost 17,000 residents.

sights.name: Mănăștur Orthodox cathedral
sights.blurb: A 62 m post-socialist cathedral (1990–2018) by Radu Spânu, built where no church was allowed before 1989.

sights.name: Gheorgheni estate and the Mercur complex (1968)
sights.blurb: Cluj’s early-1960s modernist estate and its 1968 shopping complex, still trading and visibly worn.
sights.q: Gheorgheni estate and the Mercur complex, Cluj-Napoca

sights.name: Meron Horea (Blau Palace, ex-Café Metropol)
sights.blurb: A specialty coffee bar and gallery in a 1910 palace said to have housed the Café Metropol.

sights.name: Piața Mărăști market
sights.blurb: The big neighbourhood market of Mărăști: produce, meat, cheese and a flea-market tangle of stalls. Local, not touristy.

sights.name: Central farmers’ market (Str. Ploiești)
sights.blurb: The covered produce market by Piața Mihai Viteazu: local fruit, cheese, honey, meat. The easy central one.

sights.name: The €50,000 automatic toilet
sights.blurb: A self-cleaning public WC bought for about €50,000 through the participatory budget, famous locally for breaking down.

p: The striped, onion-domed façade on Str. Horea is the Neolog synagogue, finished in 1887 and restored from 2018. You pass it on the way from Piața Mihai Viteazul to the river, so it costs you three minutes.

Its second name, the Temple of the Deportees, is the point. Cluj’s Jews were deported to Auschwitz from the town’s ghetto in May–June 1944; the building was badly damaged that year and was reconsecrated in 1951 as a memorial to them. It is one of the few visible traces of what was once a large community in the city.

Practical: exterior only unless you find it open. The Poale Tzedek synagogue (now Casa Tranzit), later on this walk, shows the other half of the story: a synagogue that lost its congregation and became an art space.

cetatuia.t: Cetățuia hill: Habsburg fort and Roth’s execution site
p: Climb the steps from the river and you are on the earth ramparts of a Vauban-type star fort, built 1715–35 to designs by Giovanni Morandi Visconti. It was the city’s first secular Baroque building, and its guns pointed at the town as much as away from it: it was built to keep Cluj under Habsburg control after the anti-Habsburg wars.

For about 200 years it served as barracks and prison. Its best-known prisoner was the Transylvanian Saxon pastor and educator Stephan Ludwig Roth, shot here on 11 May 1849 by the Hungarian revolutionary side for supporting the Habsburgs. Parts of the walls survive, with four buildings and the Water and Vienna gates; the old redoubt became the “Parachutists’ Tower”.

The giant iron cross is not old. The communists destroyed the 1702 cross in the 1950s; the present one was put up in 1995 by the nationalist mayor Gheorghe Funar, and it doubles as a political statement over a city with a large Hungarian minority.
Practical: free and open; go early in the walk, since November light fades around 16:45. Reviews note that the paths are neglected.
cetatuia.s: zcj.ro; foaiatransilvana.ro; Ziua de Cluj; Google Places

p: The long modernist slab on the south side of Cetățuia is Hotel Belvedere, built in the 1970s (Buzuloiu, Moldovan, Barabas, Spânu) as a showpiece hotel for the regime’s guests. To build it, older fort buildings were demolished: the socialist state literally put its hotel on top of the Habsburg citadel.

It is still a hotel and has changed little inside: guests describe the marble atrium, the wood furniture and a bar straight out of the period. If the lobby is open, walk in; it is the closest thing on this walk to standing inside a 1970s interior.

Comment: the report found it renamed “Transilvania” at some point; Google currently lists it as Hotel Belvedere by Unita. Radu Spânu, one of its architects, also designed the brutalist Academy Library you see later.

Enter from Strada Fără Nume, “Street Without a Name”, on the Someș bank. The plain building is the Poale Tzedek synagogue, used for worship until 1974 and then as a warehouse. Since 1997 it has been Casa Tranzit, the first synagogue in Romania turned into an art centre.

Inside, if an event is on, look up: the sanctuary ceiling is painted as a starry sky with the leopard, eagle, deer and lion of the Pirkei Avot (“be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer, strong as a lion”). Visitors mention the river running right under the windows.
Practical: the west façade was restored in 2025. Its date is disputed: local sources say 1875, Jewish Heritage Europe says early 20th century. Check eventbook.ro for what is on.

This is the building of the walk. Behind the Post Palace stands a block of exposed concrete and precast fretwork with small windows scattered as if at random. Its architect, Vasile Mitrea, called them “ferestre împușcate”, “shot windows”; locals call the building “the Silo”. Walk all four sides.

Mitrea designed it in 1968. The first three storeys went up in 1969–70 and a glass top floor followed in 1976. The window pattern was taken from the irregular windows of the old Franciscan monastery opposite, so a socialist telephone exchange quotes a medieval friary.

Its future is open. Orange fought its listing in court, so the 2020 monument order was only published in June 2025. On 7 November 2025 the city council voted 25–0 to buy it for €3.23 million; Orange has about 18 months to move out. A telecoms museum or a cultural centre are talked about; nothing is decided. BACU’s Socialist Modernism campaign lists it as endangered.
Practical: not open inside.
telephone-palace.s: Wikipedia (ro); actualdecluj.ro; Profit.ro (Nov 2025); architectuul; Socialist Modernism

p: On the north side of Piața Unirii, number 28 is where the city’s first pharmacy opened in 1573, run by the town government. A 1752 fresco inside tells the pharmacy’s history in Hungarian.
Today it is a museum of pharmacy history: old dispensing furniture, jars and medical instruments. Visitors rate it highly and say it takes about an hour, with English labels.
Practical: pass the façade on the walk; go in only if you have an hour spare.

On the west side of Piața Unirii, at the corner of Str. Napoca and Str. Universității, stand seven bronze columns over 3 m tall, each pierced with bullet holes. This is the corner where the Cluj protest broke out around 15:00 on 21 December 1989, and where 14 people were shot dead by forces defending the regime.

Liviu Mocan made the monument in 2003. Two plaques list 27 names: 26 killed and one who later took his own life. The actor Călin Nemeș was among the leaders here; he and others came out of the café of the Hotel Continental, the building right opposite.

Comment: sources disagree on where Cluj’s other dead fell (the brewery on Calea Moților, now Platinia Mall; the Astoria; Piața Mărăști), and a 2023 article counts 29 dead. No real 1989 bullet holes are known to survive in central Cluj; the holes here are symbolic. Bucharest and Brașov kept real ones.
shot-pillars.s: cluj.com; monitorulcj.ro; transilvaniareporter.ro; Gazeta de Cluj (2023)

continental.t: Hotel New York / Continental: the lost literary café
p: The big eclectic corner building opposite the Shot Pillars opened on 22 December 1895 as the Hotel New York, the first building in Cluj lit by its own power plant. Its café became the city’s leading literary and press café for more than half a century. A 2001 plaque records that the magazine Gândirea was born from the circle that met here in 1921; look for it on the façade.

Every regime used it. The Gestapo had its seat here during the Second World War; after the war it was student housing, and it reopened in the 1960s as the Continental. Writers such as Ion Mureșan and Augustin Buzura met here before 1989, and on 21 December 1989 protesters, Călin Nemeș among them, came out of its café onto the square.

Now it is shut. A businessman bought it in 2013 for €5 million and restored the façade; his company is in bankruptcy and no auction is expected before 2027. The mayor says it must stay public. Legends that Caragiale drank coffee here, or that Prime Minister Octavian Goga was poisoned in its restaurant, are unproven.
continental.s: BJC wiki; Dilema Veche; Ziarul Făclia (2026); Romania Insider (May 2026)

p: Next to the Reformed Church on Str. Kogălniceanu stands one of Cluj’s strongest brutalist buildings, the Cluj branch of the Romanian Academy Library, designed by Eliza Fierlinger and Radu Spânu in 1973–76.

The idea is readable from outside: the book stack is an armoured central core, and the reading rooms wrap around it. The structure is entirely prefabricated. Set beside a medieval church and the old university quarter, it is a deliberate socialist statement about where knowledge was kept.

Condition: the Socialist Modernism database lists it as “in use – in decay”, and a local review asks when the city will repair it. Walk-in access to the reading rooms is unverified. Optional 5-minute detour from here: the Tailors’ Bastion.

The tower at the south-east corner of the old walls is the Tailors’ Bastion, kept by the tailors’ guild and rebuilt in 1627–29. It is now a Centre for Urban Culture with small, changing exhibitions; visitors say you can climb all floors.

Behind it stands the statue of Baba Novac, general of Michael the Brave, the prince Romanians remember as the first to unite their lands in 1600. After Michael’s fall, the Habsburg general Basta had Baba Novac executed near here in 1601.
Practical: an optional 5-minute detour from the Academy Library.

Give this the most time on the walk, about 45 minutes. The city started burying its dead here, outside the walls, after the plague of 1585, and kept doing so for four centuries. Under big trees on a slope you get Hungarian nobles’ chapels, Saxon and Lutheran stones, Romanian scholars and Jewish families, layered on each other: historians call it the pantheon of Cluj.

The oldest stone, in the Lutheran section, is the 1599 grave of Felten Waida, carved “Hodie mihi, cras tibi”, “today me, tomorrow you”. Look for the neo-Romanesque Bethlen family tomb (1867), the grave of the architect Károly Kós, and the speleologist Emil Racoviță on the main west alley near the Avram Iancu gate, who links to the next stop.

It is not a tidy museum. The historian Szabó Csaba has warned of a “daily cultural massacre” as old monuments are cleared for new graves, so expect neglect and broken stones. Sources give its size as 14 or 22 ha.
Practical: main gate on Str. Avram Iancu. From 16 November it closes at 17:00. Scena Urbană has published a map of notable graves.
hajongard.s: Visit Cluj; Vasile Lechințan (academia.edu); cluj24.ro; cluju.ro

speleology.t: Emil Racoviță Institute of Speleology: the world’s first
p: A plain academic building on Str. Clinicilor, but a world first: a law of 26 April 1920 founded here the first institute of speleology anywhere. It still works in the same building, and a 1957 bust of its founder by Virgil Fulicea stands in front.

Emil Racoviță was the biologist of the Belgica expedition to Antarctica in 1897–99, the first to winter there, and then made cave life his field, running the institute with René Jeannel. You will have just passed his grave in Házsongard.
Practical: not a museum. Photograph it and move on.
The Secession-style library on Piața Lucian Blaga was built in 1906–09 by Giergl and Korb, modelled on the Basel University Library. The main reading room keeps its original desks.

The square and the library are named after Lucian Blaga, poet and philosopher, the major Romanian thinker of the interwar years. The communist regime threw him out of his university chair and silenced his publications; from about 1951 to 1959 he worked here as a librarian, in a small room next to the conference hall, and translated Goethe’s Faust there. This is the closest Cluj gets to “I sat where X sat” for a philosopher.
Practical: the building was closed to visitors from September to December 2025; check bcucluj.ro for 2026 access and tours. Google shows reader hours Mon–Sat.

The long building on the south side of Piața Lucian Blaga is the Students’ House of Culture, built 1959–60 and inaugurated on 23 August 1960, then the national holiday. It had 104 rooms and a hall of about 1,000 seats, and from 1965 carried the name of the party leader Gheorghiu-Dej.
It is still the main student venue and a concert hall; visitors find it dated inside. Together with the café Croco, opened the same year on the same square, it was the regime’s plan for student life.
Comment: the city has approved a façade clean-up, so it may look newly scrubbed.

Sit down here at the end. Croco opened in 1960 with the square and the Students’ House, and became the café where Cluj’s writers, academics, artists, journalists and taxi drivers mixed: the poets Aurel Rău and Aurel Gurghianu in the 1970s, Ion Mureșan in the 1980s. Under communism it was reportedly one of only two cafés in town serving real coffee rather than chicory.

The caveat: it closed in 2007 and became a bank branch despite protests, then reopened in 2018 as part of the Engels bistro chain, “the same, alike, but different”. So it is the same spot and name, not a continuous café. With the Continental shut, it is still the best seat in town for the Cluj literary tradition.
Practical: hours conflict between its own site and a booking site, so check. Don’t confuse it with New Croco, a pizzeria on Str. Victor Babeș. Map pin approximate (Piața Lucian Blaga 2).
croco-1960.s: croco1960.ro; monitorulcj.ro; napocanews.ro; Map pin approximate

p: The Hungarian architect Imre Makovecz designed this Reformed church in 1994–97; it was consecrated in 2008. It is organic architecture: a concrete base carrying a timber body whose interior beams curve like the ribs of a whale.
It is the nearest Cluj has to your modern-church interest. No true exposed-concrete church in Cluj turned up in the research.
Practical: Str. Donath 142, about 3 km west of the centre (bus or taxi). Reviewers often found it locked; Sunday service is the safe time to see inside.

manastur-calvaria.t: Mănăștur estate and Calvaria Church lookout
p: Mănăștur is the Falowiec of Cluj in scale, if not in form. The old village was demolished between 1965 and 1985 for workers of the CUG heavy-machinery plant; the first blocks were handed over on 2 August 1971, and Ceaușescu’s late-1970s “densification” added the towers. Planners in 1979 aimed at 120,000 residents.

In the middle, on a hill, sits Calvaria Church, an abbey church that goes back to around the 11th century, with its earth rampart still visible. It makes a lookout over the blocks: a medieval fortress-church surrounded by socialist housing.
Practical: bus 9 from the centre, about 10–15 minutes. Pair with Strada Mehedinți. Allow 60–75 minutes.
Strada Mehedinți winds through Mănăștur in an S, lined with 1970s–80s blocks; this one street alone is home to almost 17,000 people, the size of a small town.
Walk a stretch for the scale, then climb to Calvaria Church to see it from above. Map pin approximate (street centre).
On Str. Primăverii, a huge Orthodox church built from 1990 to 2018, 62 m tall, designed by Radu Spânu, co-architect of the brutalist Academy Library.
Its interest is the contrast: traditional in style, and built in an estate where no church of any denomination could be built before 1989.
Comment: the Google pin is “Saints Peter and Paul Church” on Primăverii; that it is the same building is not confirmed.

mercur.t: Gheorgheni estate and the Mercur complex (1968)
p: Gheorgheni was Cluj’s first modernist estate of the early 1960s, by Presecan, Mitrea and Buzuloiu, with ribbon windows and open staircases. The Mercur complex at Aleea Detunata 1 (Mircea Amitroaiei, 1968) was its shopping centre.

It still works as one: a small market, a supermarket, a dairy shop, a pharmacy, a gym, among crumbling walls. Socialist Modernism lists the district as “in decay” and Mercur as “inadequately rehabilitated”.
Practical: 3 km east of the centre. Interesting, but Mănăștur gives more scale for the time.
A good coffee stop near the start of the walk, in the 1910 Blau-Ullmann Palace on Str. Horea, in Meron’s former roastery, with a gallery beside the bar.
Flag: the claim that the palace housed the “Café Metropol”, a meeting place of the day’s cultural figures, comes from one lifestyle listing that names no one. Treat it as atmosphere, not history.

The everyday market of the Mărăști district: fruit and vegetables, meat, cheese and spices, plus clothes, electronics and junk stalls. Visitors describe it as an old-style market where you find everything; locals have long called part of it the “talcioc”, the flea market.
Not polished: inspectors closed parts for hygiene in 2019 and 2023, and much of the produce is imported. The city has plans to rebuild the whole area as a district centre.
Practical: 2 km east of the centre; closed Sunday; the toilet costs 2 lei.
A covered farmers’ market in a former supermarket hall by Piața Mihai Viteazu, one of the most visited markets in town: local fruit and vegetables, cheese, meat, honey, flowers.
Open every day and five minutes from the start of the walk, so it is the easy one; Mărăști is the rougher, more local one.

Not historic, but a Cluj story. Through its participatory budget the city bought automatic, self-cleaning public toilets for about €50,000 each, and the local press turned them into a running joke: “luxury toilets” at the price of a studio flat. Mayor Emil Boc defended them: a city’s public toilet is “an expression of its degree of civilisation”.
The one on Piața Lucian Blaga made the news for repeatedly not opening. Map pin approximate: somewhere on the square.
blaga-toilet.s: Adevărul; actualdecluj.ro (2023); HotNews (2018); Map pin approximate

routes.name: Half-afternoon loop: fort, concrete, 1989, cemetery, Croco
routes.when: About 3.5 h, 5 km. Do Cetățuia first: light goes around 16:45 in November. Házsongard closes 17:00 from 16 Nov.
routes.summary: From Piața Mihai Viteazul up to the Habsburg fort and 1970s Belvedere, down past Casa Tranzit to the brutalist Telephone Palace, through the 1989 corner of Piața Unirii and the Academy Library, 45 minutes in Házsongard, ending with coffee at Croco 1960.
